items.title: Emotional Work between “Reasonable Words” and “My Words”: Practices and Boundaries of Generative AI in Romantic Relationships
items.abstract: Drawing on emotion work theory and an AI-mediated communication perspective, this study uses thematic analysis to examine how emotion work is reorganized when generative AI becomes involved as a third party in communication between romantic partners. The findings indicate that some interviewees associate AI support with less concern about being judged and a lower burden of interpersonal reciprocity. They draw on its explanations and suggestions to make sense of emotions, formulate messages, and plan communication. At the same time, users need to screen and modify the generated content, and check whether the emotional attitude in it is in line with their own feelings, so as to form “authenticity work”. After the generated content is adopted, responding to the partner, fulfilling the repair arrangement, and making continuous adjustments according to the interaction between the two parties still require the input of the parties, reflecting the “limited entrustment” of emotional work. Research shows that generative AI changes the completion process of emotional work by sharing some tasks and bringing new expression management and provides an empirical basis for understanding technology-aided sincerity and relationship input.

items.title: Employment Prospect Perceptions and Learning Agency Among Chinese Undergraduate Art and Design Students
items.abstract: Background As the art and design industry faces overall pressure and employment adjustments in China, how students' employment evaluations relate to their current learning behaviors requires further investigation. Grounded in Social Cognitive Career Theory, this study examined the associations among employment prospect perceptions, career self-efficacy, outcome expectations, and learning agency. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted from April to July 2026 with 591 undergraduate art and design students from four application-oriented universities in China. A two-stage partial least squares structural equation model was employed, modeling employment prospect perceptions as a formative higher-order construct comprising absolute and comparative evaluation components, while estimating its direct association with learning agency and indirect associations via career self-efficacy and outcome expectations. Bootstrap resampling was used for inference, and exploratory comparisons across academic majors were conducted using permutation tests with Bonferroni correction. Results Career self-efficacy was positively associated with learning agency (β = .598, 95% CI [.488, .696]), and the specific indirect association from employment prospect perceptions to learning agency via career self-efficacy was .263 (95% CI [.205, .323]). The direct association between employment prospect perceptions and learning agency (β = .053, p = .239) and the association between outcome expectations and learning agency (β = .100, p = .101) did not reach significance. The model explained 48.0% of the variance in learning agency. After correction, none of the 18 between-major path comparisons reached significance. Conclusions Career self-efficacy serves as an important linking factor connecting employment prospect perceptions with learning agency. The study provides evidence for applying SCCT in career preparatory learning contexts and suggests that career support may integrate employment information with professional competence experiences. The temporal order and causal direction of these associations require longitudinal research for validation.

items.title: Empowerment, delegation and vision awareness: motivational pathways to workplace creativity
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how employee empowerment and task delegation influence workplace creativity through harmonious and obsessive work passion, and whether organizational vision awareness (OVA) strengthens these motivational pathways in a public sector context. Design/methodology/approach Survey data were collected from 533 employees across two Namibian public sector ministries using stratified random sampling. Employee self-reports were matched with supervisor ratings of incremental and radical creativity to reduce common method bias. Structural equation modeling tested indirect and conditional relationships among empowerment, delegation, work passion and creativity. Findings Empowerment and task delegation are indirectly related to creativity through distinct forms of work passion. Harmonious passion predicts both incremental and radical creativity, whereas obsessive passion is primarily linked to incremental creativity. OVA strengthens selected motivational pathways, showing that shared vision enhances the effectiveness of leadership practices in fostering creativity. Originality/value This study demonstrates that empowerment and delegation operate through differentiated passion-based mechanisms rather than uniform effects. By distinguishing between incremental and radical creativity, it clarifies how motivational processes translate managerial practices into distinct creative outcomes. It further extends the literature by identifying OVA as a boundary condition and by providing evidence from an underexplored African public sector context.

items.title: Enabling AI-ready medical graduates: A working group approach to curriculum and assessment change in a graduate medical program
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming clinical practice, and digital-health and assessment frameworks increasingly identify capabilities that involve using AI. Translating these expectations into a crowded, vertically integrated medical curriculum is a substantial implementation challenge. This case study describes how one Australian graduate medical program has approached integrating AI literacy education, teaching with AI and assessment reform. A cross-functional working group, convened by the Dean of Medicine and chaired by the first author, comprising academic, clinical, professional, library and student members and reporting to the School Executive, has coordinated the program’s early response through monthly meetings, program planning day sessions and engagement with grassroots pilots, including a trial of an AI-powered communication skills simulation platform. We describe the challenges encountered: defining AI literacy content without a settled national curriculum, negotiating curriculum space across all year levels, sustaining communication among diverse stakeholders, developing staff capability across attitudes ranging from enthusiasm to sustained concern, responding to student concerns about AI-enabled learning tools, and redesigning assessment to comply with institution-wide reform while preserving a programmatic assessment system. We share practical lessons for other programs, arguing that an enabling, relationship-centred approach may help coordinate change.

items.title: Engaging Students through Project-Based Learning during Biology Instruction in Selected Day Lower Secondary Schools in Gasabo District, Rwanda
items.abstract: This study examined how Biology teachers engage students through Project-Based Learning (PBL) in six-day lower secondary schools in Gasabo District, Rwanda, guided by three objectives: teachers' understanding of PBL, their design and implementation of PBL activities, and PBL's contribution to students' motivation.A convergent parallel mixed-methods design was adopted within the pragmatic paradigm, with all 30 Biology teachers in the six schools included through census sampling.Data were collected using a questionnaire, a semi-structured interview guide, and a classroom observation checklist, and triangulated across the three sources; quantitative data were analyzed in SPSS Version 26 using descriptive statistics and multiple regression, while qualitative data were analyzed thematically.Teachers showed a strong theoretical understanding of PBL (M = 4.00-4.13)but a comparatively weaker command of implementation and assessment procedures (M = 3.70-3.73),a gap attributed to limited time, large classes, and insufficient materials rather than to any deficit in conceptual knowledge.Effective PBL activities were curriculum-aligned, collaborative, inquiry-based, and teacher-facilitated.Authentic, real-life projects emerged as the strongest predictor of behavioral, emotional, and cognitive engagement, with the largest effect on cognitive engagement (β = 0.451, p = .001).PBL is an effective, learner-centred approach for engaging Biology students, and its full potential is currently constrained more by institutional and resource conditions than by teachers' understanding of, or commitment to, the approach.Strengthening teacher capacity in PBL implementation and assessment, and providing adequate instructional time and materials, is recommended.

items.title: Engineering Visible Thinking (EVT): A human-centred assessment framework for the Generative AI era
items.abstract: Generative AI is changing how students complete assessments and demonstrate what they know. As AI tools become part of everyday study, final assessment submissions alone may not provide sufficient evidence of how students think, solve problems, or develop understanding throughout the learning process. This paper introduces Engineering Visible Thinking (EVT), a human-centred assessment framework designed for the AI era. Rather than focusing on whether students use AI, EVT focuses on designing assessments that generate multiple forms of evidence to support judgements about student learning. The framework is built around three connected elements: visible thinking, process evidence, and capability validation. The paper draws on the design of a new Applied IT degree and includes a detailed example from the first-year Networking Fundamentals course to illustrate the application of the EVT framework in practice. The paper argues that the real challenge is not detecting AI use but designing assessments that provide evidence to support judgements about students’ learning and capability. By extending assessment beyond final products to include evidence of thinking, process and demonstrated competence, EVT offers a practical approach to assessment design that keeps people, not technology, at the centre of learning.

items.title: Enhancing cultural sensitivity in university artificial intelligence principles
items.abstract: Universities’ education-related artificial intelligence (AI) principles are vital statements that accessibly outline the institutions’ stances towards the technology’s use in learning. Ensuring the cultural sensitivity of these principles is vital given today’s superdiversity in higher education. This paper presents insights from research examining the cultural sensitivity of these principles, using Australian universities as its case study. The research covers 42 Australian universities, with AI principle content from 28 universities analysed using a qualitative content analysis. The findings show that the idea of cultural sensitivity is generally addressed at a surface level. The paper argues that all universities not only need to provide robust, publicly accessible educational AI principles, but also actively integrate cultural sensitivity into these principles. Based on the paper’s research insights, a novel framework is provided to support this integration.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Ethical Governance of AI in Public Sector Human Resource Management: Challenges of Indonesia's Digital Bureaucracy
items.abstract: The deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) has reshaped recruitment, performance evaluation, talent mapping, and workforce planning across both private and public sectors. While AI-based systems are widely associated with efficiency, objectivity, and data-driven decision-making, their use in public institutions also raises ethical problems concerning transparency, accountability, fairness, and algorithmic bias. AI systems trained on historical data can reproduce discrimination and reinforce structural inequalities. This article examines ethical AI governance in public HRM by exploring the interaction between human–AI collaboration, algorithmic bias, and institutional accountability. Using a qualitativeconceptual approach grounded in a critical literature review of 41 sources published between 2016 and 2026, complemented by analysis of recent Indonesian regulatory and institutional documents (UU No. 20/2023 on ASN, BKN Circular Letter No. 9/2025, the ASN Digital platform, and the GARUDA AI program), the study finds that Indonesia’s digital bureaucracy faces four structural challenges: a governance gap between AI adoption and regulatory readiness; limited institutional capacity for algorithmic oversight; insufficient AI literacy among HR officials; and the absence of a standardized algorithmic-ethics audit. The article contributes a four-layer ethical-governance model regulatory, institutional, technical, and capability calibrated to Indonesia’s publicadministration context, and argues that AI in public HRM must remain anchored in democratic values, social justice, and human-centred oversight.

items.title: Evaluating Generative AI in Chemistry Prelabs: Efficiency Gains without Measurable Learning Benefits
items.abstract: The rapid adoption of generative artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education has raised questions regarding their impact on students’ information literacy (IL) and cognitive processes. In this study, we investigated how generative AI influences undergraduate students’ performance and perceptions in an inorganic chemistry prelaboratory assignment consisting in gathering and elaborating information relevant to the experiments. Second-year chemistry students completed two prelab tasks: one with generative AI support and one without AI. Students reported that generative AI support significantly reduced time dedicated to prelab elaboration. They also perceived AI-assisted tasks as easier and faster, rated AI-generated information as less clear and precise than traditional sources, and frequently expressed concerns about its reliability. However, no statistically significant differences were observed in instructor-evaluated scores between AI-supported and non-AI prelabs. These results indicate that students predominantly valued AI for efficiency. Interpreted through a Cognitive Load Theory lens, the reduction in time and search effort is consistent with a possible decrease in task-related logistical demands.

items.title: Evaluating Interpretation Risks in Interactive What-If Scenarios and Mitigating with HypotheX
items.abstract: Human-centered XAI conceptualizes explanations as external representations of model behavior intended to support users’ reasoning and sensemaking, rather than as self-contained artifacts that directly convey understanding. Because their interpretation is shaped by users’ cognitive processes and contextual circumstances, understanding emerges through active engagement in formulating, testing, and refining hypotheses. In exploratory settings, where relevant questions and factors are not fully specified in advance, such engagement relies on iterative questioning, experimentation, and revision, typically mediated through interactive visualization. Hypothetical Scenario (HS)–based XAI methods operationalize this exploratory mode of explanation by enabling users to manipulate input conditions and observe resulting changes in model outputs. Through what-if testing, HS externalizes users’ reasoning processes by instantiating hypotheses as concrete interactions whose consequences become observable. Exploratory interaction, however, is not cognitively neutral. Prior work in cognitive science and human–computer interaction shows that reasoning during exploration is systematically shaped by cognitive biases such as anchoring, availability, and salience. In HS-based exploration, these biases can influence scenario selection, input sampling, outcome comparison, and the sequencing of interactions, leading to incomplete or misleading interpretations even when explanations are technically faithful. Such biases do not manifest as incorrect explanations, but as characteristic interaction behaviors that signal elevated risks of misinterpretation. Accordingly, this paper examines bias-related interpretation risks in HS-based XAI and evaluates whether targeted interface design safeguards can reduce bias-prone interaction patterns. We introduce HypotheX, an interactive HS-based XAI system, and show that interface-level interventions can mitigate some—though not all—such risks.

items.title: Exploring AI-mediated justice and fairness in collaborative learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly entering educational practice, yet its implications for justice and fairness in group work remain underexplored. This exploratory qualitative study examines 28 anonymous written responses collected from a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) on AI pedagogy and well-being involving higher-education students from five European universities. Participants responded to an open-ended question about how AI affects justice or fairness in education and group work. Using inductive thematic analysis and multi-label coding, the study identified recurring concerns around access, learning support, group-work support, contribution visibility, bias, agency, transparency and assessment. The findings should be read as a pilot mapping of fairness-related perceptions within this specific educational context rather than as representative evidence. We synthesise these perceptions into six preliminary dimensions of AI-mediated collaborative justice: access, contribution, assessment, epistemic and linguistic, agency, and transparency justice. The framework provides a starting point for future research and for the design of fairer AI-supported collaborative learning.

items.title: Exploring Trust Calibration in XAI - The Impact of Exposing Model Limitations to Lay Users
items.abstract: Trust calibration—aligning user trust judgment with model capability—is crucial for safe deployment of explainable AI (XAI), yet is often evaluated via global trust ratings detached from objective performance evidence. We present a preregistered, incentivized between-subject online study (N = 418 representative UK sample) on explainable skin-lesion classification that disentangles expectation-setting from experienced performance. Participants completed 15 case evaluations using a fixed XAI panel (malignancy score, reliability score, and saliency map). We systematically manipulated five experimental onboarding conditions varying example-based information and limitation disclosures with five stimulus packages naturally varying observed prediction quality. Calibration was operationalized as the deviation between trust-related judgments (TAIS and case-wise ratings) and objective performance benchmarks for the encountered cases, analysed with hierarchical mixed-effects models. Only limitation disclosure for case-wise measures reliably impacts trust calibration, and short-term experience did not yield progressive calibration. Further, the experienced package of stimuli explained substantially more variance than the experimental manipulation. However, participants were hard-pressed to differentiate between case-wise perceived trust, trustworthiness, and accuracy estimation. We discuss implications for designing limitation communication and for measuring and analysing calibration metrics in XAI evaluations. All study materials and data of this study are publicly available for replication and further academic use.

items.title: Faculty Adoption and Implementation Experiences During an AI Instructional Tool Pilot Test
items.abstract: The rapid expansion of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has created new opportunities and challenges for instructional practice, prompting universities to explore AI-enabled tools through structured pilot initiatives. This case study examined why faculty in the College of Agricultural and Life Science at the University of Florida chose to participate in a pilot of an AI-supported writing feedback tool and how they experienced its implementation over the course of a semester. A faculty focus group captured their motivations, perceived benefits, challenges, and recommendations for future pilots. The Theory of Planned Behavior and Diffusion of Innovations theory provided a guiding framework for interpreting faculty beliefs, social influences, and perceptions of the tool’s attributes. Findings indicated that faculty were motivated by curiosity, perceived instructional value, and alignment with institutional priorities. Implementation experiences were shaped by tool usability, course fit considerations, student response, and the availability of timely support. Participants emphasized the importance of clear onboarding, transparent communication with students, and opportunities for low‑stakes experimentation. Recommendations included strengthening training, improving integration with existing systems, and establishing ongoing feedback loops between faculty and instructional support units. The study offers practical guidance for designing AI pilot programs and contributes to emerging scholarship‑ on faculty adoption of AI tools in higher education

items.title: Feedback on feedback: Student use of AI to interpret educator feedback
items.abstract: The increasing availability of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping how students engage with learning and feedback in higher education. While existing research has largely focused on AI-generated feedback and hybrid human–AI feedback approaches, less is known about how students independently use AI to interpret educator feedback. This study investigated how Computer Science students use GenAI tools to understand and act upon educator feedback. Drawing on feedback literacy theory, an exploratory mixed-methods survey was conducted with 140 undergraduate and postgraduate Computer Science students at an Australian university. Overall, 89.0% of respondents reported using AI at least occasionally to interpret educator feedback, primarily to explain unclear comments and suggest improvements. Although students generally perceived AI explanations positively, many also recognised that AI could occasionally misunderstand educator intentions. The study contributes to emerging discussions on AI-mediated feedback literacy by conceptualising generative AI as an intermediary interpretive layer between educator feedback and student action, with implications for feedback design and the development of critical AI literacy in higher education.

items.title: Frictionless by design? Creating space for productive discomfort in interdisciplinary teaching
items.abstract: Working across disciplines requires educators and students to hold conflicting perspectives in tension, negotiate contested meaning, and integrate knowledge in ways no single discipline allows (Mansilla & Duraising, 2007). Such work is cognitively, emotionally, and socially demanding (Manathunga et al., 2006). Yet this difficulty reflects a well-established finding in education research: that struggle, effort, and a degree of discomfort are not obstacles to learning but conditions for it, provided learners feel safe enough to stay with them (Bjork & Bjork, 2011). As generative AI becomes embedded in higher education, it reshapes not only how knowledge is accessed, but the learning experience itself. This technology holds real value, yet its orientation towards fluent, instantly agreeable output can run counter to this. In practice, it smooths over the uncertainty, disagreement, and difficulty through which interdisciplinary understanding is built, narrowing the epistemic diversity such work depends on (McInnes & Airey, 2025). The question, then, is not whether to use digital tools but when – understanding where they enhance learning, and where they erode this difficulty, is a central design question for technology-enhanced learning. A key challenge for interdisciplinary educators, therefore, is how to design learning that creates space for this discomfort to thrive. While toolkits for interdisciplinary research are now plentiful, resources for teaching it remain scarce (Laursen et al., 2024). Drawing on an extensive review of the literature, we present a seven-stage model for interdisciplinary learning and teaching, spanning reflexivity, teamwork, visioning, wicked problems, disciplinary integration, creative play, and interdisciplinary assessment. The model is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs, 1996) and draws on transition-based approaches to teaching complex, real-world challenges (Bertolini et al., 2024). Originally designed around a multi-day, face-to-face interactive workshop, the model has since been translated into more practical formats: a board game version, currently being trialled, and a Canvas course in development. Across all formats, the seven stages are not about engineering discomfort but about creating a supportive, structured space in which the tensions intrinsic to interdisciplinary work can be explored directly rather than avoided or bypassed: space for sitting with not-knowing, for productive disagreement, and for the slow work of finding common ground (Colwill & Boyd, 2008). It leans on digital tools where they extend what educators can do, while keeping the work of integration and productive disagreement deliberately analogue. The purpose of this poster is to share the seven-stage model with educators and to sharpen it against the realities of interdisciplinary teaching across different disciplines and institutions. Preparing educators to teach across disciplines, not merely within them, remains an under-served challenge, and this model is a deliberate response to it. In prioritising the relational, embodied, and sometimes uncomfortable work of learning together, it offers a human-centred response to interdisciplinary teaching in an increasingly digital society – where designing for the productive difficulty that interdisciplinary work depends on is not a constraint to be managed but a capacity worth protecting.

items.title: From compliance to connection: A human-centred ethical discernment approach to ethical GenAI use in higher education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping higher education, yet institutional responses have often prioritised compliance and detection over meaningful student support. While students increasingly engage with GenAI in their learning, responsible use requires more than confidence or technical proficiency. Emerging evidence suggests students want to engage with GenAI responsibly but frequently experience uncertainty, a challenge that is fundamentally one of human-centred learning design rather than academic integrity alone. However, supporting students to become confident GenAI users cannot itself be assumed to be an ethical goal, given the technology’s potential to reproduce bias, exacerbate inequity, compromise privacy and diminish human agency. This paper proposes a human-centred ethical discernment framework grounded in connection, collaboration and compassion. Drawing on insights from qualitative research into undergraduate students’ experiences of GenAI and a practitioner-led redesign at the University of Southern Queensland (UniSQ), the framework integrates storytelling, visual pedagogy and embedded guidance, and structured dialogue to support learner agency and ethical decision making. Informed by care ethics, virtue ethics and justice, the framework positions students as accountable decision-makers capable of using, limiting or rejecting GenAI in response to context, consequence and responsibility. Rather than positioning academic integrity as a compliance exercise, the framework emphasises authentic relationships, learner agency and contextually embedded learning experiences. It offers a relational approach to supporting ethical GenAI engagement while preserving human judgement, accountability and meaningful connection within increasingly digital learning environments.

items.title: From expert feedback to AI-assisted course review: Scaling educational judgement in PAAIR
items.abstract: Monash University has embarked on an ambitious Assessment Advancement project seeing the review of over 500 courses and areas of study redesigned programmatically with intentional integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) to prepare students for an ever-changing world. The Programmatic Assessment and AI Review (PAAIR) project at Monash University is generating rich, expert feedback on course design, assessment regimes, learning outcome alignment, and AI integration across coursework programs (Baartman et al., 2022; Fawns et al., 2026; Heeneman et al., 2021; Sotiriadou et al., 2020). GenAI is intensifying the need for scalable but trustworthy curriculum review practices that preserve human agency, accountability and professional judgement. AI governance guidance emphasises that AI should augment, not displace, human agency, with human oversight, accountability and risk management built into system design (Miao & Holmes, 2023). This poster presents emerging work to use feedback from the PAAIR Panel, a cross-faculty group of Monash education experts, to train an AI agent that can support education teams in reviewing Course Design Spreadsheets as part of course reaccreditation and continuous review. The proposed AI agent is deliberately positioned as an assistant, not a decision-maker. Its role is to highlight areas within a course that may warrant closer human attention, such as unclear alignment between course learning outcomes, unit learning outcomes and assessment tasks; limited evidence of progression across a course; unclear rationale for AI use or restriction; over-reliance on particular assessment types; or places where assessment security may depend too heavily on final products rather than visible evidence of learning. The AI does not replace educational judgement, approve course design, or provide final feedback to course teams. Instead, it prompts reviewers to look more closely, ask better questions, and provide contextualised human feedback. The work responds to a key institutional challenge and a sector-wide response to enacting assessment reform in a time of AI: how to scale educative feedback across large numbers of courses while maintaining the professional judgement, disciplinary sensitivity and care that meaningful course review requires (Lodge et al., 2025). By training the agent on feedback authored by Monash education experts, the project seeks to preserve and amplify local educational expertise rather than outsource it. The AI is being designed to support consistency, reduce reviewer workload, and make recurring patterns visible across submissions, while keeping humans responsible for interpretation, dialogue and decision-making. Achieving these aims without compromising feedback quality is a high priority in our testing. This approach contributes to broader conversations about responsible AI in higher education by exploring a human-in-the-loop model where AI assists educational teams to review complex curriculum data. The AI supports the review while decisions stay with educators. The model could transfer to institutions following a similar review process, though their policy, curriculum templates and staffing will shape feasibility. The poster will share the emerging design principles, potential workflow, and early opportunities for using expert-informed AI to support programmatic assessment and AI integration.

items.title: From grading to learning: Reconsidering assessment for learner agency through institutional practice
items.abstract: As generative AI reshapes how learners access, generate and engage with knowledge, the tertiary education sector is increasingly developing assessment approaches that better cultivate learner agency, meaningful engagement with feedback, and self-regulated learning. Alongside these developments, longstanding debates about the role of grades have gained renewed prominence, prompting greater attention to how assessment systems support learning, certification, and learner agency. This paper presents an institution-wide exploration of ungraded assessment as one approach to designing assessment that places greater emphasis on dialogue, learner agency, and meaningful feedback. The focus extends beyond evaluating a single assessment model to examine how the University’s central educational practice team, college and school learning and teaching specialists, and academic staff collaboratively explored the relationships between grading, feedback, and learning across different disciplinary contexts. Drawing on practice-informed examples, the paper illustrates how different contexts interpreted and adapted ungraded assessment, from studio-based pedagogies in design to emerging experimentation in computing balancing developmental learning with progression requirements. The paper argues that designing assessment with foregrounds dialogue, learner agency, and meaningful feedback cannot be achieved through assessment task redesign alone; it requires coordinated curriculum, educator capability, and institutional practices. It identifies practice-informed design considerations to strengthen learner agency and sustainable assessment reform in AI-enabled higher education.

items.title: From prompt to practice: A visual framework for AI-supported creative learning in animation education
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how students imagine, produce, revise and communicate creative work. In animation education, AI tools can support rapid ideation, visual experimentation and alternative design pathways, but they also raise questions about how students continue to develop foundational skills, creative judgement, peer critique and reflective practice. This poster presents a classroom-informed visual framework for integrating AI into practice-based creative learning without reducing learning to prompt generation or final outputs. The framework was developed through practice-led curriculum redesign in an undergraduate animation course. It is informed by reflective practice, foundational animation principles, authentic learning, engagement theory and recent debates about AI in higher education (Bearman et al., 2023; Herrington, 2006; Kearsley & Shneiderman, 1998; Schön, 1983; Thomas & Johnston, 1981). Rather than positioning AI as a replacement for craft, critique or student decision-making, the framework maps AI-supported creative learning as an iterative studio process: observe, experiment, generate, critique, reflect, refine and share. This cycle visualises how AI can be embedded within classroom activities while keeping human judgement, feedback, revision and ethical decision-making central to learning. The poster focuses on how this framework can support creative practice in the classroom. It highlights how students may use AI to explore visual possibilities, test ideas, compare alternatives and reflect on their decisions, while still being assessed on process, reasoning, feedback use, authorship and responsible tool engagement. The visual model is organised around four pedagogical commitments: reflection; iteration; collaboration and critique; and ethical decision-making. By foregrounding a practical classroom case and a visual teaching framework, this poster contributes to ASCILITE 2026’s themes of connection, collaboration, creativity and compassion in a digital society. Although grounded in animation education, the model offers transferable strategies for educators designing AI-supported learning in creative, project-based and practice-based courses.

items.title: From short-term gains to deep learning: Designing AI learning agents through productive failure
items.abstract: This conceptual paper proposes a conceptual framework for designing Productive Failure-informed AI learning agents that function as pedagogical facilitators rather than answer-providing tools. Grounded in Productive Failure (PF), the framework structures AI-supported learning across three interconnected phases: idea generation and exploration, consolidation, and knowledge assembly. Within each phase, it specifies the role of the AI facilitator, the structure of AI–learner interaction, and the cognitive processes intended to support learning. The framework positions AI agents as mediators that activate prior knowledge, encourage multiple solution attempts, support comparison with canonical knowledge, promote recognition of knowledge gaps, and guide the organisation of emerging understanding into generalisable principles. Theoretically, the framework extends PF into AI-mediated learning contexts by translating its underlying mechanisms into interaction design principles. Practically, it provides educators and developers with a pedagogically grounded approach to designing AI-supported environments that prioritise cognitive engagement, conceptual understanding, and knowledge transfer. Future research should empirically examine the framework across disciplinary, learner, and institutional contexts.

items.title: From tools to sense-making: Designing a human-centred AI workshop
items.abstract: Generative AI raises identity- and values-level questions for higher education staff. Yet professional development in this space remains largely focused on individualised technical and pedagogical skill and capability development, rather than providing structured opportunities for the collective sense-making such questions require. This paper describes the design and delivery of a human-centred workshop developed for a team of higher education third space practitioners to support collective sense-making and values negotiation around AI use. Drawing on reflective practitioner inquiry, we describe the design principles that shaped the workshop and the practical constraints within which it was delivered. We reflect on what worked, including the value of structured formats in supporting deeper engagement, and of workshop artefacts as an evolving record of shared thinking. We suggest this design offers a transferable approach for other educator teams grappling with similar uncertainty, and propose that professional development for AI should complement skills-focused approaches with structured space for the collective exploration of values, judgement, and human agency.

items.title: From tools to teammates: When children and AI create together in early childhood education
items.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence becomes increasingly integrated into learning environments, its role is shifting from a passive tool to an active partner in meaning-making and creative expression. This study explores how young children engage in co-creative learning with AI through adults and examines the implications of these interactions for reimagining human–AI partnerships in early childhood education. Sixteen children (aged 5-6) from a single preschool classroom first drew an original character and then worked individually alongside a researcher to generate an AI-based version of that character using Gemini, with up to three iterative prompts per child. Data from classroom observations, interaction records, and reflective discussions were analysed using thematic analysis to understand children’s interaction dynamics. Initial findings reveal one key dimension of co-creative engagement. Children appreciated AI’s ability to extend and transform their visual ideas, yet emphasised the importance of maintaining personal authorship and manual control, highlighting an emerging sense of creative agency in human–AI collaboration. Building on these findings, the study proposes a vision of AI as a creative teammate that amplifies children's imagination while preserving human intentionality and ownership.

items.title: GenAI avatars to promote negotiation and AI skills among student presentations
items.abstract: The rapid proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has radically disrupted higher education assessment paradigms (Chung, 2024). Institutional responses to maintaining assessment integrity have primarily focused on defensive mechanisms, such as mitigating risks surrounding written assessments, refining text-matching software, and enforcing restrictive academic integrity policies (Lodge, 2024). However, this reactive posture often overlooks the transformative potential of GenAI as a student’s and lecturer’s long-term coach in authentic assessment design (Atif, 2024). This research-in-progress pivots away from deficit-based AI detection, proposing instead the integration of VirtualSpeech GenAI avatars to converse with students during a recorded viva, generating verifiable, real-time student output. By replacing static written tasks with dynamic oral assessments, this relatively new form of creative expression maintains authentic student contributions to improve AI literacy, strengthen authorship verification, eliminate academic outsourcing, and simultaneously cultivate sophisticated negotiation skills (Perkins, 2026). This study represents an exemplary innovation of practice by reframing AI not as an academic threat, but as a dual-mode learning and assessment avatar. Rather than engaging with AI purely for text generation, students interact with GenAI avatars (such as VirtualSpeech) simulating realistic corporate stakeholders. This work is strongly anchored in the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework, which guides the deliberate alignment of GenAI technology, modern pedagogy, and discipline-specific knowledge (Mishra & Koehler, 2006). This framework assists educators in leveraging immersive technology to redefine pedagogical delivery, facilitating AI literacy and negotiation skills. This research addresses a critical gap in current Technology Enhanced Learning (TEL) literature by investigating the following central question: How are students’ AI literacy and negotiation skills developed when conversing with GenAI avatars as part of a viva presentation? Adopting a design-based research methodology, this project emphasizes the iterative refinement of an educational intervention within an authentic setting (Hoadley & Campos, 2022; Scott et al., 2020). The study is currently in its first implementation cycle within a major tertiary institution, featuring a sample size of 150 second-year Project Management students. Participants are required to defend a project proposal during a live, assessable viva presentation conducted with a customized VirtualSpeech avatar trained to act as a client. This oral format diminishes the appeal of cognitive offloading because students must defend their reasoning under unseen, real-time questioning (Sotiriadou et al., 2020; Tan, 2026). Data collection relies on a mixed-methods approach, utilizing pre- and post-intervention surveys alongside qualitative analysis of student reflections. Preliminary quantitative results indicate a statistically significant increase in both self-reported IT literacy, validating the avatar’s efficacy as a formative and summative tool. This research significantly advances TEL research and practice by providing a protocol for proactive AI integration. While piloted within a project management curriculum, broad applicability across tertiary contexts exists (Cela-Ranilla, 2025). Any discipline requiring high-stakes communication, critical thinking, and stakeholder management—such as business, law, or education—can adapt this viva model. Ultimately, this work demonstrates how universities can safeguard academic integrity not by restricting technology, but leveraging it to create robust, future-focused verbal assessments, requiring students to perform and defend understanding live.

items.title: General intellect y gestión algorítmica. La regulación del trabajo en plataformas digitales
items.abstract: This article analyses transformations of work under cognitive and platform capitalism, placing algorithmic management at the centre as a contemporary form of labour control. Through a critical dialogue with technological determinism, it draws on Castells and Vercellone to explain how knowledge and workers’ cognitive capacities have become central sources of capital valorisation. Within this framework, algorithms operate not as neutral technical tools but as sociotechnical devices that organise, supervise and discipline labour in a continuous, opaque and delocalised manner. The article shows how platform companies condense long-term historical tendencies by articulating concentrated digital infrastructure, large-scale data capture and narratives of individual autonomy. Analysis of the mechanisms of algorithmic direction, evaluation and discipline demonstrates that control over the labour process shifts towards the appropriation of collective knowledge, that is, of the general intellect. Finally, the article examines the regulatory frameworks of Spain and the European Union, the four Latin American cases currently in force, and ILO Convention No. 193, adopted in 2026. items.title: Generative AI and Audit Quality in Jordanian Listed Industrial Companies
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may support audit work, but its association with audit quality depends on how auditors use and evaluate its outputs. This study examines task–technology fit, quality-oriented utilization, professional judgment quality, and digital competence among 214 external auditors serving Jordanian listed industrial companies. Respondent-level averaged indicators were analyzed using a reflective measurement model and regression equations corresponding to PROCESS Models 1, 4, and 7. Audit-firm size and professional certification were included as covariates. Reflective discriminant validity was supported by HTMT values of 0.587–0.660. Across 5,000 bootstrap samples, the indirect association through professional judgment was 0.115 (95% CI [0.078, 0.159]). Conditional indirect associations increased from 0.048 at low digital competence to 0.154 at high competence; the index of moderated mediation was 0.082 (95% CI [0.043, 0.126]). The findings are consistent with a professional-judgment pathway and a competence-related boundary condition. They support further evaluation of task suitability, verification practices, and competence development. Cross-sectional self-reports, aggregated indicators, and incomplete independent validation of formative composites limit causal interpretation and generalization. JEL classification numbers: M42, M15, O33. Keywords: Generative artificial intelligence, External audit quality, Task-technology fit, Professional judgment, Digital competence, Jordan.

items.title: Generative AI and Cognitive Autonomy in Cameroonian Higher Education: A Conditional Amplification Framework for Learning
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is rapidly entering higher education, yet its implications for learner autonomy remain unsettled, particularly in resource-constrained contexts. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined how pedagogical GAI use relates to self-regulated learning, cognitive engagement, augmented cognitive autonomy (ACA), and deep learning in six Cameroonian higher education institutions. Quantitative data from 812 students and faculty members were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling, followed by 24 semi-structured interviews. GAI use was positively associated with self-regulation, while self-regulation and cognitive engagement sequentially mediated its relationship with ACA. ACA was strongly associated with deep learning. AI literacy and institutional governance strengthened the relationship between GAI use and ACA. Qualitative findings revealed both reflective, dialogic uses and cognitive delegation. The findings support an emerging Augmented Cognitive Autonomy framework in which GAI amplifies learning conditionally, depending on users' regulatory capacities and institutional support, with implications for equity and human capability development.

items.title: GST Compliance Reconciliation and Vouching Verification in a Small Chartered Accountancy Practice: An Applied Case Study from India
items.abstract: Goods and Services Tax (GST) compliance and vouching are usually taught as separate subjects, one belonging to indirect taxation and the other to auditing. In small Chartered Accountancy (CA) practices in India, however, the same junior staff perform both, on the same client files and within the same monthly cycle. This paper examines how the two work-streams complement each other as an integrated, reconciliation-first assurance process. Using a single-case, participant-observation design, it draws on an eight-week on-the-job training placement (22 June to 22 August 2026) at a mid-sized CA practice in Maharashtra, India. Process observations, a structured learning diary and template-based working papers were used to document the monthly GST compliance cycle and a transaction-level vouching routine. Because client information is confidential, the analysis uses an anonymised, illustrative entity whose figures were constructed to reflect patterns observed in practice. In the illustration, outward supplies matched fully across the sales register, GSTR-1 and GSTR-3B, while an Input Tax Credit (ITC) mismatch of ₹7,200 in April, caused by a supplier's late filing, fell to ₹4,500 in May and cleared by June. An eleven-voucher vouching sample produced two exceptions, both procedural. The paper argues that vouching and GST reconciliation test the same books against two different evidence sources, so that errors escaping one check tend to be caught by the other. It closes with recommendations on standard checklists, named ownership of reconciliation and a shared mismatch tracker, and discusses limitations arising from the single-firm, short-duration and illustrative-data design. Keywords: Goods and Services Tax; Input Tax Credit; GSTR-2B reconciliation; vouching; audit evidence; chartered accountancy practice; workplace learning

items.title: How Price Shocks Moderate Pro‐Environmental Social Norms for Sustainable Consumption
items.abstract: Price inflation is a major and urgent consideration for consumers and governments around the world. This study measures how price shocks moderate pro‐environmental social norms and sustainable consumption. By combining the insights from a local survey on social norms and panel regression results from a large national survey, the study shows how price shocks in relation to energy, food, and water change social norms (descriptive and injunctive). The analysis also identifies a dynamic relationship between price and pro‐environmental social norm changes and their translation into behaviour. The new phenomenon not studied previously leads to the stipulation of ‘price norm theory’. Financial incentives via price change drive both a rational economic and a social norms response. This important and novel insight is relevant to understanding the influence of inflation and economic incentives on sustainable consumption. Policymakers can change pricing and financial incentives and influence social norms (in addition to consumer benefit–cost ratios).

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration and Sustainable Business Model Innovation with Platform Dependence
items.abstract: Digital platforms provide entrepreneurial firms with resources while constraining their strategic discretion. Drawing on paradox theory, this study examined associations between respondents’ human–AI collaboration (HAIC), paradoxical cognition (PC), ecosystem hybrid orchestration capability (EHOC), platform dependence (PD), and reported sustainable business model innovation (SBMI). We analysed 379 matched single-informant records collected in China in March and April 2026, with a mean interval of 23.92 days. The analysis used categorical controls, HC3 inference, formal shape tests, and 5000 bootstrap resamples. HAIC exhibits significant negative curvature in relation to SBMI, but the upper-bound slope test is borderline (one-sided p = 0.05002); the strict inverted U shape is therefore not robustly confirmed. The HAIC-squared term is not statistically significant in the executive subsample, and formal interaction tests do not establish a difference between respondent groups. The serial indirect association through PC and EHOC decreases between low and high HAIC, whereas the EHOC-only pathway increases, and the total indirect difference is not significant. PD negatively moderates the EHOC–SBMI association in the linear model; an exploratory quadratic specification reveals a more complex boundary. The findings distinguish cognitive and resource-coordination associations in a single-informant observational design.

items.title: Human–AI Collaboration and Value Co-Creation in Digital Ecosystems: A Theory-Driven Systematic Review and Research Agenda
items.abstract: Purpose: This review synthesizes evidence from recent studies of human–AI collaboration in service and digital ecosystems to build and test a multi-level conceptual framework. Design/methodology/approach: Thirteen studies (Tier A) from 2024 to 2026 were analyzed in full text and compared with 25 qualitative and mixed-methods studies (Tier B). In total, 38 service and digital ecosystem studies were analyzed within this review. Service-Dominant (S-D) Logic and the Affect–Behavior–Cognition (ABC) model was used as the underlying theoretical framework. Narrative and thematic analysis were employed to synthesize the results from the included studies. Findings: Transparency, process control and outcome control have significant effects on employees in terms of cognitive and behavioral effects, while system-initiated engagement has little effect. Human–AI interaction does not, on average, perform better than the best human in each task (g = ?0.23, p < .001), but does perform better than a single human in a variety of tasks (g = 0.64). Value is created through the integration of systems and not through technology itself. User experience, digital maturity, interoperable IT, and AI-induced technostress condition value realization. Originality/value: The study provides a three-stage framework, seven testable hypotheses, seven gaps in current research and an operational measurement for value creation at the employee level and for firm- and network-level value co-creation.

items.title: Human–AI risk decision-making: The effects of risk-taking tendency and transparency design
items.abstract: This study investigated how artificial intelligence (AI) risk-taking tendencies and transparency design influence human risk-taking behavior, trust in AI, and neural activity in risky decision-making contexts. Drawing on previous findings of human–AI collaboration and social influence, we examined human–AI interaction during the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) to measure cerebral activation. The study employed a 2 × 2 between-subjects design (risk-taking vs. conservative AI; transparent vs. non-transparent design). A total of 120 participants completed the task under one of four experimental conditions. Behavioral results showed that participants initially increased their risk-taking behavior when paired with risk-taking AI, but gradually reverted to baseline, indicating increasing risk-aversion over time. Conservative AI did not significantly reduce risk-taking behavior below baseline, though it elicited higher trust ratings. Contrary to predictions, similarity in risk-taking tendency did not significantly enhance trust. Transparency design accelerated risk-aversion toward risk-taking AI and reduced trust bias toward conservative AI. Neuroimaging results revealed decreases in prefrontal and temporoparietal junction oxygenated hemoglobin, consistent with cognitive offloading when AI advice was present; these effects were attenuated under the transparent condition, suggesting sustained engagement. Overall, findings highlight the dynamic nature of human–AI risk decision-making and underscore the role of transparency in calibrating trust and maintaining user involvement in risky decision-making tasks.

items.title: Immersive simulation-based learning with virtual prototypes: advancing student engagement and educational quality in engineering
items.abstract: Purpose Immersive learning environments have been widely recognized for their potential to support student engagement in engineering education; however, their adoption is often constrained by high costs and limited accessibility. This study aims to examine the use of low-cost virtual prototypes as an alternative to high-cost immersive learning technologies in higher engineering education, with particular emphasis on accessibility and sustainability. Design/methodology/approach A one-group quasi-experimental pretest–posttest design was implemented with a sample of 92 undergraduate engineering students in a Latin American university context. Student engagement was assessed using a validated multidimensional instrument based on the Burch Engagement Survey for students framework, capturing physical, emotional and cognitive dimensions. Given the presence of both matched and unmatched observations, engagement differences were analyzed at the dimension level using statistical methods appropriate for partially overlapping samples, with effect sizes and confidence intervals reported to support interpretation. Findings The results showed pre–post increases in physical engagement and, to a lesser extent, emotional engagement after the intervention. In contrast, no statistically significant changes were found in synchronous or asynchronous cognitive engagement. These results suggest that virtual prototypes may be associated primarily with active participation, while deeper cognitive engagement may require additional scaffolding, reflection and metacognitive support. Originality/value This study contributes to the discussion of accessible engineering education by providing evidence on low-cost immersive tools and by identifying potential connections with sustainability-oriented educational goals. While the findings may align with goals of inclusion and equity in Sustainable Development Goal 4, they should be interpreted cautiously due to the study’s design. The results offer practical insights for technology-enhanced learning environments and future research directions.

items.title: Improving Explanations: Applying the Feature Understandability Scale for Cost-Sensitive Feature Selection
items.abstract: With the growing pervasiveness of artificial intelligence, the ability to explain the inferences made by machine learning models has become increasingly important. Numerous techniques for model explainability have been proposed, with natural-language textual explanations among the most widely used approaches. When applied to tabular data, these explanations typically draw on input features to justify a given inference. Consequently, a user’s ability to interpret the explanation depends on their understanding of the input features. To quantify this feature-level understanding, Rossberg et al. introduced the Feature Understandability Scale [ 49 ]. Building on that work, this proof-of-concept study collects understandability scores across two datasets, proposes a co-optimisation methodology of understandability and accuracy and presents the resulting explanations alongside the model accuracies. This work contributes to the body of knowledge on model interpretability by design. It is found that accuracy and understandability can be successfully co-optimised while maintaining high classification performances. The resulting explanations are considered more understandable at face value. Further research will aim to confirm these findings through user evaluation .

items.title: Influência da inteligência artificial nos processos cognitivos: atenção, memória e tomada de decisão
items.abstract: The progress of digital technologies, particularly artificial intelligence, has been transforming everyday life by acting as a support for cognitive processes such as attention, memory and decision making. With the growing use of technology and easy access to information, a change in human behavior can be noticed: instead of memorizing content, people prioritize quick access to it, which raises doubts about the effects on critical thinking and intellectual autonomy. Research such as that of Sparrow et al. (2011) suggests that the internet makes it easier to remember where to find information, rather than concentrating on retaining the content itself. Risko and Gilbert (2016) discuss cognitive "offloading" to technological devices, which may reduce mental effort. Simon's (1955) theory of bounded rationality helps to understand decisions made under cognitive limitations, a context in which AI can act as a support resource. Given this, the aim of this study is to analyze how artificial intelligence influences attention, memory and decision making, seeking to understand whether its use favors cognitive optimization or may cause negative long-term impacts. It is a qualitative, exploratory and descriptive literature review that gathered 21 works. The studies indicate that frequent and unreflective use of these tools may favor the transfer of cognitive tasks to external resources and excessive trust in AI responses, but the evidence on attention comes from digital technologies in general, and research on generative AI is still scarce and, to a large extent, preliminary. Better performance on a task done with AI does not, by itself, amount to learning.

items.title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
items.abstract: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

items.title: International students and cross-cultural adaptation in China: A latent growth model of positive affectivity and relationship-building
items.abstract: The herein presented latent growth model, grounded in the integrative communication theory, examines how international students’ trait positive affectivity relates to cross-cultural adaptation through proactive general socializing and networking. A four-wave longitudinal study of 140 international undergraduate students in a Chinese university revealed that positive affectivity is positively related to psychological adaptation and negatively related to sociocultural adaptation difficulty, and that it predicts improvement in both outcomes over time. General socializing and networking showed distinct mediating roles in these relationships, with socializing explaining changes in psychological adaptation and networking explaining changes in sociocultural adaptation difficulty. By modeling adaptation trajectories with latent growth analysis and focusing on proactive relationship-building behaviors that expand access to social and informational resources, the study contributes to a more dynamic understanding of cross-cultural adaptation and suggests practical strategies for universities wanting to help international students adapt to new cultures.

items.title: Islamic Ethical Leadership and Employee Innovative Work Behavior in the AI Era
items.abstract: Universities are increasingly requiring their employees to be innovative, with a growing reliance on new digital tools, but it remains to be seen how innovation can be fostered by leaders demonstrating Islamic ethical values (justice, trustworthiness, consultation, truthfulness, and excellence) and whether the involvement of employees in the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace will make a difference. The present research involved 465 academic and administrative staff of public and private universities in eight cities of Pakistan. Based on social learning and social exchange theories, it mapped out the relationship between employees' perceptions of their leaders' behaviors and their perceptions of how safe they felt expressing unfinished ideas, and then how often they generated, championed, and implemented new ideas, and examined whether trust in the use of AI tools affected this process. A coherent picture began to emerge. Leaders who were described as fair, trustworthy, and consultative were seen to create a safe environment for others to share their ideas, and this created a small but strong influence on innovation; a direct leadership relationship still existed. Trust in AI was correlated with increased innovative behavior on its own, but did not obviously increase or decrease the relationship between psychological safety and innovative behavior; it seems that the two resources operated independently. The pattern was confirmed after adjusting for demographic factors and for institutions. Psychological safety then becomes a partial conduit for values-based leadership; AI trust becomes an additive but not a conditioning resource, but a single-source, single-time design can't establish causation.

items.title: Job Autonomy, Cognitive Load and Technology Adaptation Behaviour in Small and Medium Enterprises: A Moderated-Mediation Framework
items.abstract: Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) in emerging economies are introducing digital tools faster than they are redesigning jobs around them. Job autonomy is the work design lever most often recommended for this transition, yet evidence on its effect on employees' technology adaptation behaviour is mixed. This conceptual paper integrates cognitive load theory with self-determination theory to explain why. It argues that autonomy supports technology adaptation through motivation but, beyond a certain level and under complex tasks, also raises the working-memory demands of learning new systems, so that cognitive load partially offsets its benefits. The paper proposes a moderated-mediation model in which cognitive load mediates the autonomy–adaptation relationship, task complexity shapes the autonomy–load link, and digital leadership acts as a boundary condition on both the direct and indirect paths: leaders who combine a learning orientation with clear structure are expected to lower the load that unstructured discretion creates. Generational cohort is treated as a proxy for prior digital experience rather than as a fixed trait. Six propositions, one of them in two parts, are derived and a survey-based research design for Vietnamese SMEs is specified, including measures, a two-wave data collection protocol and a partial least squares estimation strategy with quadratic and conditional indirect effects. The framework offers HRM researchers a testable account of when autonomy helps or hinders adaptation, and offers SME managers a rationale for calibrating autonomy and leader structure during technology roll-outs rather than maximising either.

items.title: Keeping humans in the loop: AI-assisted curriculum at program scale
items.abstract: As universities adopt generative AI for curriculum development, a central risk is that efficiency gains may come at the expense of educational judgement, disciplinary expertise and human connection. Yet the same technology, used selectively, can free academics to focus on how students think and solve problems (Truu, 2026). This poster presents a programmatic, human-led method for AI-assisted course development used across UNSW College’s new Applied Degrees: industry co-designed, work-blended bachelor programs in business and information technology. It addresses two questions: how can generative AI support curriculum development at program scale while preserving human educational judgement; and where must that judgement be structurally embedded? The method is grounded in constructive alignment (Biggs & Tang, 2011) and human-centred AI (Le Dinh et al., 2025), applied at program rather than course level. The main focus is programmatic coherence. Rather than building courses one at a time, the method applies shared design patterns across an entire program. Even with different subject matter experts (SMEs) and program leads contributing to different courses, these design principles remain consistent from first year to capstone. AI generates content within this architecture, but functions as a structured design assistant rather than an autonomous author. Different workflow stages route to different AI models suited to each context. This preserves checkpoints where human framing and contextual judgement re-enter the process, consistent with calls to keep human control central to AI in education (Alfredo et al., 2024; Bearman et al., 2023; Hau, 2025; Islam, 2026). The human-led, AI-supported workflow moves from industry and academic SME input and course overview revision through curriculum blueprinting, assessment critique, rubric development, Canvas-ready asynchronous content, workshop planning, and student-facing resources. The assessment-critique stage is especially significant as generative AI reshapes what assessment must do, with recent scoping evidence showing AI is driving a re-examination of assessment design across student, teacher and institutional levels (Chiu et al., 2024). Human judgement remains decisive throughout: SMEs establish disciplinary intent; program leads review coherence and progression; learning designers evaluate scaffolding, accessibility and learner experience; and final quality assurance confirms alignment before publication. The ASCILITE Technology Enhanced Learning Accreditation Standards (TELAS, 2022) informed the design from the outset and now provide the basis for review, making quality auditable. This matters for Applied Degrees, where quality depends on integrating academic standards, industry relevance, work-integrated learning and inclusive learning design. Outputs are structured for continuous improvement in Canvas, keeping pedagogical authority close to the point of delivery rather than locked inside opaque AI outputs (UNESCO, 2023). Critically, automating the repetitive build frees human effort for the work most often skipped under time pressure: the programmatic view, gathering student feedback, time with industry to collect current case studies and simulations, and targeted employability development so graduates are work ready. AI can accelerate curriculum production while strengthening human-centred design, provided the architecture and its checkpoints are designed first. The contribution is that architecture. The design patterns, curriculum blueprinting and checkpoints where human judgement re-enters are transferable to other program-scale builds regardless of which AI tools are used.

items.title: Latent profiles of artificial intelligence ethical awareness and their association with professional identity among nursing interns: A multicentre cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Background: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated into nursing education and clinical practice, nursing interns need to recognise and address ethical issues associated with its use. However, heterogeneity in their AI ethical awareness remains poorly understood. This study aimed to identify latent profiles of AI ethical awareness among nursing interns, examine factors associated with profile membership, and compare professional identity across profiles. Methods: A multicentre cross-sectional study was conducted among 550 nursing interns from 12 hospitals in China between September and October 2026. Data were collected on sociodemographic characteristics, AI ethical awareness, attitudes towards AI use in nursing, ethical sensitivity, and professional identity. Latent profile analysis was performed using the mean scores of six AI ethical awareness domains. Profile characteristics were compared using chi-square tests and Welch's analysis of variance. Factors associated with profile membership were examined using R3STEP multinomial logistic regression, while differences in professional identity were assessed using the Bolck–Croon–Hagenaars method. Results: Three profiles were identified: consistently low awareness (C1; n = 152, 27.6%), autonomy–education salient (C2; n = 232, 42.2%), and consistently high awareness (C3; n = 166, 30.2%). The three-profile model demonstrated the lowest AIC, BIC, and sample-size-adjusted BIC, with an entropy of 0.876. Educational level, prior AI-related education, AI familiarity, AI tool-use frequency, attitudes towards AI use in nursing, and ethical sensitivity were associated with profile membership in at least one pairwise comparison ( p < 0.05). Attitudes towards AI use in nursing and ethical sensitivity were associated with all three pairwise comparisons. Professional identity scores were lowest in C1 (59.06 ± 7.77), intermediate in C2 (61.15 ± 8.14), and highest in C3 (63.33 ± 7.89). Significant differences were observed across profiles (Wald χ² = 23.739, p < 0.001), with all pairwise comparisons remaining significant after Holm adjustment. Conclusions: A one-size-fits-all approach to AI ethics education may not adequately address nursing interns' diverse learning needs. Nursing educators could consider tailored educational strategies that emphasise critical evaluation of AI-generated information and ethical issues related to transparency, accountability, and algorithmic fairness. Further longitudinal research is warranted to clarify the relationship between AI ethical awareness and professional identity. Clinical trial number: Not applicable.

items.title: Leadership as an AI Governance Capability: A Contingency Model of Effective Human Oversight and Human, AI Complementarity
items.abstract: Assigning a human reviewer to an AI-assisted decision does not ensure meaningful oversight. Reviewers also need the evidence, authority, and time to identify errors and secure appropriate corrections. Building on Ouchen, Chouay, and El Arabi’s (2026) account of leadership as a governance capability, this article develops a contingency model of how those conditions can be established. The model links responsibility boundaries, decision orchestration, and collective learning to three mechanisms: calibrated reliance, actionable contestability, and verified learning feedback. Their expected effects depend on task evaluability, error detectability, review resources, and incentives.

items.title: Learning Companion for students’ critical reasoning and academic writing
items.abstract: The advent of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) transformed technology’s role in the education sector by introducing highly adaptive, interactive tools. Standard implementations are often inadequately designed to effectively aid students. In some cases, these systems hinder genuine learning by inducing cognitive offloading, offering immediate solutions that bypass the cognitive processes necessary for deep conceptual understanding. This concern highlights the need for pedagogically grounded systems that foster genuine understanding and skills development. To address this gap, this paper presents an experimental implementation evaluating the feasibility of embedding formal educational frameworks directly into AI system architecture. We introduce Learning Companion, a prototype engineered to mitigate passive cognitive offloading by translating educational theory into programmatic workflows. Rather than replacing educators or automating learning, the Learning Companion is designed to strengthen meaningful learning interactions by positioning AI as a collaborative partner that supports learner agency through guided dialogue and adaptive instructional scaffolding. Aimed at enhancing critical reasoning and academic writing, the system operationalises Vygotsky’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) through algorithmic Socratic questioning to provide structured instructional scaffolding. This human-centred approach demonstrates how AI can complement teaching and foster deeper learner engagement while preserving meaningful connections between students, educators, and intelligent learning technologies.
